sense: the principles of a subject, as against practice

evidence: Caes. BG 4.1.6: ratiō atque ūsus bellī
terms.comment: Latin sets ratiō or scientia against ūsus, practice (Caes. BG 4.1.6; Cic. Rep. 1.2).

evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.2: scientiā tamen ipsā tenērī potest

terms.gloss: an art, its rules and principles
evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.2: ars quidem, cum eā nōn ūtāre

terms.comment: Cicero writes it in Greek (Att. 12.6.1: Lewis & Short); in Latin from Jerome on. Morgan–Owens gives it for theory as against practice.

phrases.latin: Nec vērō habēre virtūtem satis est quasi artem aliquam, nisi ūtāre; etsī ars quidem, cum eā nōn ūtāre, scientiā tamen ipsā tenērī potest, virtūs in ūsū suī tōta posita est
phrases.english: Nor is it enough to have virtue as one has some art, unless you use it; for an art, even when you do not use it, can still be held by knowledge alone, but virtue lies wholly in its use

phrases.latin: Sīc neque agrī cultūra nec ratiō atque ūsus bellī intermittitur.
phrases.english: So neither farming nor the theory and practice of war is ever broken off.

sources: Lewis & Short: ratio · Lewis & Short: scientia · Lewis & Short: ars · Lewis & Short: theoria
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. practical: theory.
Cicero (Rep. 1.2) and Caesar (BG 4.1.6) checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
